paragraphs: Most of the remarks I have already made about servants and masters may be applied to masters and workmen. As the gradations of the social scale are less and less observed, as the great sink while the humble rise, and as poverty, like opulence, ceases to be hereditary, the distance that once separated the workman from the master, in reality and in opinion, shrinks every day. The workman forms a loftier opinion of his rights, his future, and himself; he is filled with new ambition and new desires, and troubled by new wants. At every moment he looks with longing at his employer’s profits, and in order to share in them he tries to sell his labor at a higher rate, and generally succeeds in the end. In democratic countries, as elsewhere, most branches of productive industry are run at small cost by men whose wealth or education raises them little above the level of those they employ. These manufacturing speculators are extremely numerous; their interests differ, so they cannot easily act in concert or combine their efforts. The workmen, on the other hand, almost always have some sure resources that allow them to refuse work when they cannot get what they consider a fair price for their labor. In the constant struggle over wages between these two classes, their strength is divided and success passes back and forth. It is even probable that in the end the interest of the working class must prevail, for the high wages they have already won make them less dependent on their masters every day, and the more independent they grow, the easier it is for them to win a further increase in wages.

I shall take as my example the branch of productive industry that is still, today, the most widely followed in France and in almost every country in the world — I mean the cultivation of the soil. In France most of those who labor for hire in agriculture own small plots of ground themselves, which are just enough to support them without working for anyone else. When these laborers come to offer their services to a neighboring landowner or farmer and he refuses them a certain rate of wages, they withdraw to their own small property and wait for another opportunity.

I think that, on the whole, it may be asserted that a slow and gradual rise of wages is one of the general laws of democratic communities. As social conditions become more equal, wages rise, and as wages become higher, social conditions become more equal. But in our own time a great and gloomy exception occurs. I showed in an earlier chapter that aristocracy, driven out of political society, has taken refuge in certain departments of productive industry and set up its rule there in another form; this has a powerful effect on the rate of wages. A large capital is required to embark on the great manufacturing speculations I have in mind, so the number of people who enter them is extremely small. Because they are few, they can easily act together and fix the rate of wages as they please. Their workmen, by contrast, are extremely numerous, and their number keeps growing; for from time to time an extraordinary rush of business occurs, during which wages are excessively high and draw the surrounding population into the factories. But once people have taken up that way of life, we have already seen that they cannot leave it again, because they soon acquire habits of body and mind that unfit them for any other kind of toil. These men generally have little education and industry, and few resources; they therefore stand almost at the master’s mercy. When competition or other chance circumstances reduce his profits, he can lower his workmen’s wages almost at will and make up from them what he loses to the chances of business. If the workmen strike, the master, being rich, can easily wait, without being ruined, until necessity brings them back to him; but they must work day by day or die, for their only property is in their hands. Oppression has long since impoverished them, and the poorer they become, the more easily they can be oppressed: they can never escape this fatal circle of cause and effect. It is not surprising, then, that wages in this branch of industry, after sometimes rising suddenly, are lowered for good; whereas in other callings the price of labor, which generally rises only a little, nevertheless keeps going up.

This state of dependence and wretchedness, in which part of the manufacturing population of our time lives, is an exception to the general rule and runs contrary to the state of all the rest of the community. For that very reason, no circumstance is more important or more deserving of the lawmaker’s special attention. When the whole of society is in motion, it is hard to keep any one class standing still; and when most people are opening new paths to fortune, it is no less hard to make the few bear their wants and desires in peace.
